report:
Conclusion: a firm “yes” is not supported. The rationale is plausible—statins can lower circulating CoQ10—but clinical evidence for relieving statin-associated muscle discomfort is inconsistent. A Mayo Clinic Proceedings meta-analysis of randomized trials concluded there was no significant benefit of CoQ10 for statin-induced myopathy and called for larger, better trials: https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/article/S0025-6196(14)00799-X+/fulltext. A key double-blind trial enrolled patients whose symptoms were confirmed by a statin/placebo crossover, making false attribution less likely; it is central to the skeptical evidence: https://www.atherosclerosis-journal.com/article/S0021-9150(14)01636-0/abstract. The American Heart Association’s statin-safety statement similarly notes CoQ10 has been proposed, but RCT evidence is not supportive: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/atv.0000000000000073.

There are newer meta-analyses reporting reduced pain/weakness/cramps, e.g. a 2025 systematic review says supplementation “can reduce muscle pain” but still stresses more research is needed: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12554813/. Those positive signals are limited by small trials, differing doses/formulations, heterogeneous symptom definitions, and no consistent creatine-kinase effect.

Bottom line: CoQ10 is generally safe and reasonable to discuss as a time-limited trial after checking interactions and ruling out serious myopathy, but the evidence does not justify a confident claim that it relieves statin muscle discomfort. Persistent pain, weakness, dark urine, or marked CK elevation warrants prompt clinical review rather than self-treatment.
